Read mortgage ratios alongside the take-home budget: two views of the same housing decision

Use four charts to compare assessed debt-service ratios, actual housing bills and the cash left after everyday spending and planned saving.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Read the assessed ratios beside a separate take-home budget

Interactive planning lab

Monthly cash remaining after the planned saving$50

Original monthly comparison beside CMHC’s published reference ratios, reviewed 25 October 2026. This does not issue a mortgage qualification, pre-approval or affordable home price. Gross income, net income, actual mortgage P&I and qualifying mortgage P&I are independent inputs: no tax conversion, amortization, stress-test payment or income eligibility is calculated. The assessed housing amount includes qualifying P&I, property tax, heat and 50% of condo fees. TDS adds the independently assessed other-debt obligation, which can differ from actual repayments. The separate cash budget uses actual P&I, full condo fees, all entered other home costs, actual other debt, non-housing living costs and planned saving against take-home income. Costs must not overlap. No default-insurance premium, down payment, credit decision, loan-to-income restriction, rental offset, ground rent, variable-income review or exceptional underwriting rule is modeled. Negative remaining cash is an unfunded monthly budget, not an available overdraft. The 39% / 44% references are scoped to the cited material and are not universal approval promises.

The central idea

Keep the lender’s assessed payments and gross-income ratios beside an independent household cash budget. Each view reveals a different constraint.

01

Write down which question each calculation answers

Mortgage planning involves more than finding a payment a calculator will accept. An underwriting ratio compares specified obligations with income under a lender’s assessment. A household budget asks whether the actual cash arriving can cover the home, everyday life, debt repayments and saving. A decision can look comfortable in one view and tight in the other.

The tool keeps those views side by side. Gross annual income is used only in the ratio calculation. Monthly take-home income is entered separately for the cash budget. It does not convert one into the other or estimate an income-tax return.

FCAC’s mortgage-preparation guidance discusses income, housing costs, debt and the household budget. The charts develop an original example from independently entered values. They do not check a credit file, verify income or make an application decision.

02

Use assessed obligations consistently in the ratios

Gross debt service, or GDS, compares the assessed housing amount with gross income. Total debt service, or TDS, adds assessed other-debt obligations. The tool expresses annual income monthly so numerator and denominator cover the same period.

For the cited comparison, CMHC publishes 39% GDS and 44% TDS references. Its housing treatment includes qualifying principal and interest, property taxes, heating and half of applicable condominium fees. Those references are held fixed in the chart and were reviewed on 25 October 2026.

The default assessed housing total is CAD 3,850 monthly: CAD 3,200 qualifying principal and interest, CAD 300 property tax, CAD 150 heat and CAD 200 from half of the full CAD 400 condo fee. Against CAD 10,000 gross monthly income, GDS is 38.5%. Adding CAD 500 of assessed other debt makes TDS 43.5%.

These are original example calculations. Actual income acceptance, debt assessment and other conditions need confirmation with the applicable lender and insurer. The tool takes the assessed other-debt obligation as an input rather than assuming that every contractual minimum is the amount used in underwriting.

03

Keep the assessed payment separate from the payment you expect to make

A qualifying payment can be calculated at a rate above the mortgage contract rate. The tool therefore asks for actual principal and interest and qualifying principal and interest separately. Neither amount is derived from the other here; both should be independently checked when a real mortgage is being considered.

As reviewed on 25 October 2026, OSFI describes the minimum qualifying rate for uninsured mortgages as the greater of the contract rate plus two percentage points or 5.25%. It describes application to most newly underwritten residential mortgages at federally regulated lenders.

OSFI also identifies an exception for qualifying uninsured straight switches between federally regulated lenders at renewal, without an increase to the loan or amortization. This article does not determine whether a case meets that exception or another rule. Do not use a new-borrowing illustration to infer the requirements of every renewal or transfer.

04

Pay the full bill in the household cash ledger

The ratio’s treatment of part of a cost does not reduce the actual bill. The cash waterfall therefore includes the full condo fee, actual mortgage payment and entered property tax and heat. It also includes other non-overlapping home costs, such as insurance or maintenance, that the household needs to fund.

In the default budget, CAD 7,500 of take-home income funds CAD 3,700 of housing costs, CAD 500 of other repayments, CAD 2,500 of non-housing living costs and CAD 750 of planned saving. Only CAD 50 remains. Both displayed ratios are below the cited reference percentages, yet this example has very little unused monthly cash.

Each cost should appear once. Put other home costs outside the tax, heat and condo amounts already entered. Put non-housing living expenses outside debt repayments and saving. If an assessed debt amount differs from the actual repayment, retain the distinction instead of forcing one number into both calculations.

05

Inspect payment room and budget flexibility together

The income curve asks how much qualifying mortgage principal and interest fits within both reference ratios after the selected assessed obligations. It is payment room, not a mortgage principal amount, a house price or a pre-approval. Turning it into a loan amount would require an independently checked rate, amortization and other financing inputs.

The budget matrix asks a separate question. It changes take-home income and everyday living costs while preserving gross income and the assessed obligations. The GDS/TDS ratios therefore stay unchanged, even though the amount of actual cash remaining can move from a surplus to a shortfall.

Use the two views to frame the next review: verify the assessed inputs, fund closing costs separately, check irregular home expenses, and test whether saving and an accessible reserve remain feasible. A negative budget needs an explicit response. A positive one still needs review against real payment dates and costs that may be missing from the first draft.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. Charts labelled “Official statistics” or “Derived from official statistics” identify their source periods. Other charts are hypothetical scenarios. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

  1. CMHC · Calculating GDS / TDS ↗

    Public ratio definitions and 39% / 44% references reviewed 25 October 2026. The model is a limited arithmetic illustration, not a complete mortgage-insurance assessment.

  2. OSFI · Minimum qualifying rate for uninsured mortgages ↗

    Page modified 29 January 2026 and reviewed 25 October 2026. Supports the described rate and straight-switch qualification. The tool does not calculate a qualifying payment or decide whether an exception applies.

  3. FCAC · Preparing to get a mortgage ↗

    Public consumer guidance dated 15 October 2025, reviewed 25 October 2026. Context for checking debt, income and affordability; all household amounts shown here are hypothetical.
